q: forget why i entered a room
forget what i was doing when i walk through a door
why do i forget why i entered a room
forget why we entered a room
forget what we were doing when we walk through a doorway
a: The doorway effect (also known as the location-updating effect) is a psychological phenomenon where walking through a doorway triggers a forgetting of what you were about to do or think about. Research suggests that doorways serve as 'event boundaries' that segment our continuous experience into discrete episodes. When we pass through a doorway, our brain treats the new room as a new event, and the previous room's context is cleared from working memory. This is believed to be an adaptive cognitive mechanism that helps us organize our continuous experience into meaningful chunks. The effect was systematically studied by researchers like Gabriel Radvansky at the University of Notre Dame, whose experiments showed that people were significantly more likely to forget information after walking through a doorway compared to walking the same distance in a straight line. The effect is not limited to physical doorways - virtual doorways in video games and even imagined boundaries can produce the same forgetting effect.
